adds.title: Gender Recognition in Mexico by State | Human Rights Watch
adds.summary: HRW's state-by-state table (31 Mar 2025) records that Tamaulipas 'has not reformed its legislation to create a legal gender recognition procedure for transgender people', placing it among the eight Mexican states with no procedure at all, against 22 of 32 states that have legislated an administrative procedure (two more have one in practice only). For a trans person whose documents are issued in Tamaulipas this means there is no administrative route to change identity documents to match their gender identity, which is the record's core claim.

adds.title: Aprueban en Tamaulipas sanciones contra terapias de conversión y ataques a la identidad de género - NT | Noticias de Tampico Tamaulipas
adds.summary: On 18 June 2025 the Tamaulipas state Congress unanimously approved reforms to the local Penal Code adding a chapter on crimes against sexual orientation, gender identity or gender expression, explicitly banning 'conversion therapies' with prison terms of 2-6 years and fines of up to 2,000 UMA; penalties rise by half when victims are minors, disabled or elderly, or in subordinate settings such as family, medical or workplace. Dated evidence that Tamaulipas's criminal law protects gender identity even though the state still lacks an administrative gender-recognition procedure.

adds.title: Comunidad LGBT+ y diputadas acuerdan agenda conjunta por identidad de género y salud en Tamaulipas - NT | Noticias de Tampico Tamaulipas
adds.summary: On 4 February 2026 deputies of Tamaulipas's 66th legislature and LGBT+ civil-society groups (including Tamaulipas Diversidad, Vihda Trans A.C., Tendremos Alas A.C. and La Resistencia Trans) agreed a joint agenda to push a Gender Identity Law and anti-discrimination and health reforms, noting the initiatives have been pending since June 2025 and that the absent law keeps limiting trans people's access to health, education and employment. Confirms that as of early 2026 no legal gender-recognition procedure exists in Tamaulipas and a Gender Identity Law remains unpassed.

quality_summaries.rewritten_summary: HRW (31 Mar 2025) reports that 22 of Mexico's 32 states have legislated an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, that eight states have no procedure at all and two more have one in practice without being enshrined in law; the article's state table lists Tlaxcala among the states WITH a procedure - its Congress passed a 2019 reform to the Civil Code creating an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition. The record's claim that Tlaxcala is 'not among the states whose legislatures have enacted no legal gender-recognition procedure' is therefore supported (though HRW's count of states without a procedure is eight, not six), and the article contains no Tlaxcala-specific ordinance beyond that 2019 reform, nor any Tlaxcala-specific incident or enforcement data.

HRW (31 Mar 2025) reports that 22 of Mexico's 32 states have legislated an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, that eight states have no procedure and two more have one only in practice; the article's state table lists Yucatan among the states WITH a procedure - its Congress passed a 2024 reform to the Civil Registry Law creating an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition. The record's claim that Yucatan is 'not among the states whose legislatures have enacted no legal gender-recognition procedure' is therefore supported (the true count of states without a procedure is eight per the source, not six), and the source contains no Yucatan-specific incident series or enforcement pattern data beyond that 2024 reform.

adds.title: LGBT rights in Nigeria - Wikipedia
adds.summary: The English Wikipedia page 'LGBT rights in Nigeria' sets out the federal framework under which Taraba sits: same-sex sexual activity has been illegal since 1904 in the Northern Region and since 1916 region-wide, and penalty is up to 14 years' imprisonment under federal law, the Same-Sex Marriage Prohibition Act 2014 criminalising all forms of same-sex unions as well as registering or publicly promoting gay organisations. The page lists harsher Sharia-law penalties (from lashing or caning up to death) only for states that have adopted Sharia; Taraba is not named among them, matching this record's finding that no Taraba Sharia application is documented. The page contains no Taraba-specific statute or incident; it serves as the national-framework document the state's visitor stands under.

adds.title: Tell Me Where I Can Be Safe: The Impact of Nigeria's Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act | Human Rights Watch
adds.summary: Human Rights Watch's report of 20 October 2016, 'Tell Me Where I Can Be Safe: The Impact of Nigeria's Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act', records that the SSMPA, signed into law on 7 January 2014, imposes prison terms of 10 to 14 years on anyone who operates, participates in or supports gay clubs, societies or organisations, and finds that its passage was immediately followed by mob attacks, arbitrary arrests, extortion and detention of LGBT people across the country, including the arrest without charge of 21 young men at a birthday gathering in Ibadan and repeated police detentions reported by interviewees elsewhere. The report is national in scope and names no Taraba-specific case, but it substantiates the federal criminalisation and arbitrary-enforcement climate on which Taraba's visitor assessment rests.
